first.rationale: The two symptoms actually degrading (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) point at the funnel itself, not at price. Promotional pricing is the tempting response to the competitor, but memory_73 carries its own explicit caveat: it buys acquisition while materially damaging 30-day retention and should not be generalized. Against a primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, that is a revenue-shaped loss, so I am declining it despite the competitive pressure. Onboarding simplification (memory_86, memory_31) is the one direction that plausibly addresses both declining metrics at their root, since completion feeds activation; activation_messaging (memory_91) treats only the downstream half. Referral incentives (memory_57) are clean but target established customers, not the leaking self-serve funnel; enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44) is a different segment entirely and does not touch the observed decline. I am spending both verification pulls on the memories my chosen action actually rests on rather than on the one I am rejecting: memory_86 and memory_31 are consolidated summaries from days 52 and 12, their sources are archived, and I cannot see from the summary alone whether the lift was measured on activation only or carried through to qualified revenue, nor whether the day-12 SMB result still holds under a changed competitive mix. Explicit downstream risk: 'cutting required fields at signup' improves activation by removing exactly the qualification data used to route prospects, and memory_44 says enterprise converts through sales-assisted demo paths. A field-cut that lifts self-serve activation could quietly starve enterprise pipeline quality, which is where the durable qualified revenue lives, so the headline metric would improve while the objective degrades. I therefore scope this as a small guarded test with a holdout, instrumented on downstream qualified revenue and enterprise routing rates rather than completion alone, and I keep enterprise-relevant fields intact. If the archive shows either memory measured revenue rather than activation proxies, I would widen to a standard experiment; if it shows the day-12 lift was activation-only or on a segment unlike today's, I would fall back to activation_messaging, which carries less qualification-data risk.

mid.rationale: Both pulls came back confirmed and both strengthened the case. exp_86 is the stronger record than its summary suggested: completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, and 30-day retention +3%, so shortened onboarding is not a retention-neutral activation trick, it improves the thing the objective actually cares about. exp_31 measured qualified revenue directly at +4% with retention only -1%, which meets the escalation condition I set in advance, so I widen from a small guarded test to a standard experiment. This remains the only candidate that addresses both degrading metrics at the root, since completion feeds activation, and I hold my rejection of promotional_pricing: the competitor's entry pricing is real pressure but memory_73's retention damage makes it a revenue-shaped loss against a sustainable-revenue objective, and nothing in this cycle changed that. Two limits keep me off broad rollout. First, exp_31 is explicitly 'holds on SMB; not replicated on other segments,' so the qualified-revenue result is an SMB result and I scope the experiment to SMB self-serve rather than treating it as a general funnel truth. Second, my flagged downstream risk is unresolved rather than cleared: neither source record measured enterprise pipeline quality, so the concern that cutting required signup fields removes the qualification data feeding the demo-request path in memory_44 is simply unmeasured, not disproven. I therefore preserve enterprise-relevant routing fields, leave the enterprise sales-assisted path untouched, and instrument on downstream qualified revenue and enterprise routing rates alongside completion, with a holdout. The -1% retention in exp_31 versus +3% in exp_86 also suggests signup-field cuts and flow-shortening are not the same lever; I lead with flow-shortening, which carries the cleaner retention evidence, and treat field reduction as the narrower, more closely watched component. If enterprise routing degrades or qualified revenue fails to track completion, I stop and fall back to activation_messaging (memory_91), which touches only the downstream half and does not disturb qualification data.

final2.rationale: I am holding the decision. The competitor's second cut is the same pressure at higher intensity, and intensity is not new evidence. Nothing arrived this week that touches the one fact that disqualified promotional_pricing: memory_73 records that it materially reduced 30-day retention and carries an explicit instruction not to generalize it as a growth strategy. Against a primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, discounting into a price war with a competitor who has already shown willingness to cut deeper would buy back exactly the accounts most likely to churn, at worse retention, and would concede the pricing floor. That is a revenue-shaped loss dressed as a response, and doubled churn conversations make the retention penalty more costly, not less. The verified evidence still favors the current plan and is stronger than it was on day 76: exp_86 shows shortened onboarding lifting completion +13% with 30-day retention +3%, and exp_31 shows qualified revenue +4% on SMB. Improving time-to-value is a defensible answer to price pressure, since accounts that reach value fast are the ones a discount cannot easily poach. I keep the standard experiment scoped to SMB self-serve, because exp_31 explicitly did not replicate on other segments. I also keep the unresolved flag: neither source record measured enterprise pipeline quality, so the risk that cutting required signup fields starves the demo-request path in memory_44 remains unmeasured rather than disproven, and I preserve enterprise routing fields and instrument on downstream qualified revenue and enterprise routing alongside completion. Stated honestly for leadership: this does not stop churn conversations this week, and I am not claiming it will. Onboarding is a root-cause fix on a slower clock, and the single slot does not carry over, so spending it on a lever with known retention damage would cost both the slot and the retention. Retention and pricing objections are better met with non-experiment work outside this slot: direct save conversations with at-risk accounts, and memory_57's referral incentive, which added qualified revenue without measurable retention harm, as the honest fallback if I am overruled or if next week's evidence shifts. I would revisit promotional_pricing only with a fresh archive pull showing the retention penalty was segment-specific or time-bound.
